## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it. An entry's history is part of that search, and is read before any claim about the entry's reasons, since the history keeps the ground and the curator's words that the entry's text leaves out.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- A worker that looks for issues gives all its findings the same weight. Sort the findings yourself, by what each needs, before any finding reaches the curator or goes into the next brief:
  - If a finding would change a decision of the curator's, put it to the curator as an ask. No other finding becomes an ask.
  - If a reason in the record is no longer true, cut it. You need no approval to bring the record in line with reality.
  - If a finding corrects the ground of an entry and changes no decision, put it in the entry's history. It changes nothing that a reader does.
  - If a finding confirms a decision, give it one line.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Have the skill writer add, change or remove a rule of this skill, in `SKILL.md` or in a part, only after a cold read of the change (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). A fix of a path or a section name is a change too, except at an approved draft's landing (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). The writer's fixes of the cold read's flags land with no second cold read. Then the change lands without the curator's yes, also when you proposed it, unless the bullet after next says that it waits. A line of `references/sources.md` is not a rule, and needs neither a cold read nor a report.
- After a change to this skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts or the page of `fortress-repo` changes, whose links the boot note holds (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). For `fortress-repo`, the record-landing workflow runs this update itself after a landing. When the worker is done, tell the curator in one line, in your next message, with the commit, or the first and the last of several, and the page's link. Watch both pages for comments sent to Claude. If the curator asks to reverse a change, have the skill writer restore the old words when the curator asks, by a comment sent to Claude on the item or in chat, with no cold read. The reversal does not wait for the end of the curator's reading. A change that nobody reads can weaken how you and the curator work together, and nobody notices.
- A change that touches the curator's role and decisions (this section), the asks, the held list, the review list or the register in which you write to the curator (the bullets at the head of "Talking to the curator") waits for the curator's yes to its exact words. So does every rewrite of this skill's `SKILL.md` or of a whole part of this skill, since it can touch any rule. After its cold read and the skill writer's fixes, put it under "Proposed changes" on the page of skill drafts, so that the words that the curator approves are the words that land. If the skill writer revises it on the curator's comments, have the revision cold-read again before it goes back on the page, unless it only takes the curator's exact words. Such a change has no default: it stays out of the skill until the yes. If you are unsure whether a change touches these, it waits.
- Change the other skills by the method of `references/skill-rewrite.md`. No change of them waits for the curator's yes, a change of their `SKILL.md` or a new rule included. Each lands after its cold read and the skill writer's fixes. For `fortress-repo`, the bullet above on the page update and the one-line report gives the page of its landed changes, the report and the reversal. For `cloud-container`, tell the curator in chat when a change lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for. If the curator asks, reverse it as that bullet says. So that the curator notices a new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, name it as such at the head of the chat line. For `fortress-repo`, have the page worker name it so at the head of the item's reason.

## 2. What the clause does for the checker and the library today

1. **The checker reads a `comprises` clause in eight places.** I read the Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/`:
   - The closure check. Each type that extends a closed trait must be below a listed type, or be a closed trait whose listed types all are, or be a generic trait whose known extenders all are. Otherwise: "Invalid comprises clause: ... is not eligible to extend it".
   - Exclusion. Two types exclude each other when no value has both. The checker proves it four ways: an `excludes` clause; a `comprises` clause, where a closed trait excludes a type that excludes every listed type; an object, which excludes every type that it is not below; and the exclusion rule. With `Number` closed, `Number` excludes any type that excludes all five listed types. A program's own object is such a type. So is `MultiplicativeRing[\Cx\]` for a program's `Cx`, by the exclusion rule against each listed type's own ring.
   - Subtyping into a union. A closed trait is below a union when each listed type is.
   - Meeting types. In an intersection, a closed trait is replaced by those of its listed types that the other parts do not exclude. So under the clause, `Number & AdditiveGroup[\Cx\]` is empty.
   - The Meet Rule. Where the parameter types of two overloads overlap and neither is below the other, a declaration must cover the overlap. Several declarations can cover it together, the closed trait read as the union of its listed types.
   - Abstract methods. An object can define an inherited abstract method by several narrower bodies that together cover it, through the clauses.
   - The type of `self`. In a trait with a clause, `self` has the type of the trait met with the union of its listed types.
   - The export check. The api's clause and the component's clause must match.
2. **Dispatch does not read the clause.** The code generator says that the clauses "should not affect code generation once type checking is complete". The compiled dispatch has no reference to exclusion or to `comprises`. A second "closed type" rule, in `ExclusionOracle.scala`, is not in use: no code makes an `ExclusionOracle`, and the class is named only by two imports.
3. **Walk reads clauses too.** Walk's exclusion test reads the clauses transitively, down to objects. Its overlap reading cuts a type by its clause in two places. The library's reflective QuickCheck reads a type's clause at run time to choose a type to generate.

## The principle for the batches

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1303`, batch rule 1).

    The failures past U+FFFF come from two gaps of the parser, both in one rule, `UnicodeHexChar`. Its first choice takes four or five upper-case or decimal digits, its second the same in lower case, and its third and fourth `10` and four digits. The parser commits to the first choice that matches, and does not come back to try another when the closing mark then fails to follow. So for `'10FFFF'` the first choice takes `10FFF`, and for `'1000a'` it takes `1000`; in each case a digit stands where the closing mark must be [11]. Two kinds of code fail:

They include assigned characters, as U+1000A, LINEAR B SYLLABLE B057 JA, U+1300A, EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPH A008, and U+2000A, a CJK ideograph.

    Every failure that the sweep listed is of these two kinds, and the sample's 6,857 is the count that the rule gives for it. A brief holds what only you know: the problem, the question, what the answer is for, and where the sources are. Give the readings that the task needs and no more, and an order or steps only where they matter. A worker on the repository has `fortress-repo` loaded, and that skill loads the parts that the work needs. So leave the choice of those parts to the worker. Each extra reading costs your context, and the worker chooses well without it.

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- For a review, an ask to sort its findings by what each needs. The reviewer names each finding that would change a decision of the curator's, and gives options for those findings only.
- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
- The entries that it needs, by number. If the task needs an entry's linked entries or its history, name `facts-extract.sh`, which prints them. Quote whole, with its limit and its example, only a rule of the curator's that no entry holds yet.
- The people of the project by name and role, as the record and the authorship map `research/authorship.md` name them, never in your own words, since a worker copies your description into its text; where the task needs who wrote what, a pointer to the map.
- Before you quote the curator's words from a message, clean them. Fix the obvious typos of the phone's swipe keyboard and of dictation, and keep the meaning. Put `[?]` after each word whose reading is a guess.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 240 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

`fortress-repo` tells a worker on the repository which choices are its own. A worker loads no part of this skill by itself. If it does part of your work, such as an analysis, name the parts of this skill that the work needs.

## Judge and repair round

A judge runs on a rung only on a contested fix, a refusal or a worker's stop, and on the merged tree only on a blocking review or a red gate. It builds and tests nothing. It writes `JUDGE.md` (on the rung's branch, or `JUDGE-<kind>.md` in the batch's folder) and commits it.

- On contested fixes it rules on each listed fix alone: uphold, or revert it itself with `git revert --no-edit`, which takes the fix's test with it. Its decision is `stands`, `repair` (numbered instructions for one round), `drop` or `stop`.
- On a refusal, the same four.
- On a stop, `repair` means the stop is not one: the worker resumes and its skeptic follows. Any other decision leaves the rung stopped.

Its brief carries its question, the contested fixes with both arguments, and the worker's decisions. It points to the checks slice, each fix's commit and the sections of `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` it needs. In batch 10 a judge's brief carried the worker's whole result and the skeptic's verdict, two thirds of its 61K tokens, and the judge used about 30% of them (`process-engineering/checking-roles-cost.md`, section 2).

A first ruling on a rung or the merged tree runs on Opus; a second on the same one on Fable (`judgeTier`; the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The roles", and `references/delegating.md`, "Which tier runs what").

A repair round is the rung worker again, with the checks slice, the judge's decision and the rung's section. It carries out the instructions in order, test first, and updates `REPORT.md` and `record.md`, whose texts replace the worker's; its structured result replaces the worker's too, so it describes the whole rung as it now stands. No skeptic follows it: its own test, the review and the gate check it. A repair that does not land drops the rung. No second repair round is taken.

## Gather

The gather composes one local commit per approved rung on `main`; nothing is merged.

- **The order.** First, a rung goes after every rung it lands only with (`landsOnlyWith`), so that no commit on `main` holds a rung without the rungs it needs: in climb batch 17 the old rule, which compared lines across files, put rung L's `2b1cd8e63` before rung W's `743eb5286`, and that commit alone fails `LibraryOverloadFamilies.fss:37` (`reviews/batch-17-review.md`, finding 2). Then the rungs that share a file go in the ascending order of their lowest edited line in that file, so that a later hunk does not shift lines a landed record cites; a line is compared only with a line of the same file, and rungs that share no file keep the manifest's order. Where two files order one pair both ways, the pair keeps the manifest's order. Any `file:line` a record cites that an earlier hunk shifted is re-anchored by symbol. Tests cite the specification by section, never by line, so no test is re-anchored.
- **Each rung.** Its net diff is applied with `git apply --3way --index`. A conflict in unrelated regions is resolved by hand; one in the same logic is returned, not guessed. Its files are written from the journal where the branch lacks them, by the commands the brief renders per rung. For a repaired rung, `REPORT.md` and `record.md` are always rewritten from the repair round's texts.
- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. A ledger note that adds a fact through `ledger.py note`. A change to what a row says (its claim narrowed, a half fixed, its test promoted or renamed, its notes at the limit) through `ledger.py rewrite N FILE`: the whole line, stating the gap as it stands now, not its repair history. A note refused for length goes in so, with the notes cut back; none is left out. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line, in the batch's `RECORD.md`, "Handover lines" (the old handover file is retired into PLAN's first section, which the coordinator keeps). The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. Each sentence of the specification a rung lists as made false and did not edit, corrected to what the code does, each clause checked against its code line. Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Appendix I Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false. Each took a review judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6).
- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).
- **Items for the curator.** The gather puts every item a rung, skeptic or judge returned into `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when work waits on it, else under "Off the path, parked".
- **After the rungs.** The landed rungs' walk tests run on the merged tree in one `harness-one.sh` call, each `X.test` named beside its `X.fss`: climb batch 26's gather ran its 20 twice, the first call without the five `.test` files (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 7). One commit closes each row a landed rung fixed (`ledger.py close N --commit HASH --test NAME`, then `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, which fails on any finding, also one the base already had; each is cleared through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or the entry reworded, before the commit). A row whose test is the checker count or the distance stage closes on the rung's run of it, the gate's tables its check: the gather runs neither stage. In climb batch 25 it ran the distance stage for row 873 on code the gate measured again (`reviews/batch-25-review.md`, finding 6). One commit writes the batch's `RECORD.md`, once, last: the order and why, each rung's commit, the rows opened and closed, each skeptic's fixes and the contested rulings by commit, the rungs that did not land, the points to report, where each item for the curator went, and last, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer", each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both parts word for word.
- **The specification's PDF.** When the gather builds the specification to check its text, it builds it once, on the text after the last edit under `Specification/`, and keeps the PDF at `tmp/gather/fortress-batch-<N>.pdf` in the main tree, which the commit stage takes ("Commit, and the push held", step 1).

A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.

Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before each commit. A commit touching a path outside `explorations/` and `.claude/` carries a `historical:` line.

## Review beside the gate

The review and the gate start together on the gather's commits. The review reads and never builds; the gate builds and never reads the record; the gate commits nothing, so the two never commit at once. Run side by side they took 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The review stays, once (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). Its six checks:

1. Overlaps between rungs, and what their changes do together.
2. Each skeptic's fix and each repair commit, as applied: it does what its finding says, its test seen failing on the worker's head and then passing in its maker's transcript, a settled fix's citation, a reverted fix gone.
3. The folded record: FACTS lines, `ledger.py landing-check BASE` with no finding, also none the base already had, each fixed in the review's corrections commit, no `NEW-` placeholder left where a row is cited, every closed row fixed, the handover, the revival-change material in `RECORD.md` true of the landed code.
4. Each specification sentence a rung listed as made false, corrected.
5. The points to report, with `holdsPush`.
6. The items for the curator, in `PLAN.md`.

What it does with a finding:

- A record-only or mechanical defect it fixes itself, inside `explorations/`, in one commit.
- A finding settled by tests and records only it routes to the next batch, as `review-routed.N` in `PLAN.md`, with no judge.
- A finding whose repair touches source, library, checker, interpreter or specification goes to a judge, who rules `land`, `repair`, `drop` or `stop`. `land` is for a ruling settled by tests and records after all: its steps go to the next batch and no repair runs.

The review returns its heads before and after its corrections and every path outside `explorations/` they changed. A path the gate reads makes the gate beside it stale, and the gate runs again. Any other path is recorded beside the gate's summary.

A review that returns nothing after three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and `review-missing.1` is listed.

### A review that still blocks after its repair

There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.

### A repair of tests and records only

After a repair on the merged tree, the review's or the gate's, the whole gate runs again only when the repair, or the review's corrections, changed a path the gate reads that is not a test file: under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml` (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs", and `fortress-repo`'s `references/gate.md`, "When to run it"). In batch 8 the gate ran a second time after a repair of one sentence of Appendix I, 24 minutes on the critical path, with tables identical but for timing (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 4).

A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.

- The repair returns its heads and changed paths. In `testRuns` it lists each test file it added or changed, run in the harness on the merged tree: the files of one corpus together in one JVM (`ONE_JVM=1 junit.sh`, and one `harness-one.sh` call for the interpreter tests).
- The gate runs again on a code path, a changed test no passing run exercises, a run that failed, or a repair that listed nothing.
- After the gate's repair it also runs again unless every red line is answered by a passing run (`failingAnswered`) and no suite count fell.
- When a red gate stood beside the review, and the review's repair of tests only answers its lines, no gate judge or gate repair runs.
- When the first gate's tables stand, the commit stage appends the runs to `summary.txt` as `# repair-tests` lines, and the paths no stage reads as `# repair-ungated` lines. `gate_compare` skips `#` lines.

`repairRerun` in the script decides.

## Gate

One run on the merged tree, its logs under `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, its three outputs written by fixed functions, never by hand. The functions of steps 5 and 7 (`gate_summary`, `gate_compare`, `last_landed_summary`, `ladder_filter`, `ladder_compare`, `mg_phases`) are in `tools/gate-functions.sh`, which the gate sources from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set; until 2026-10-10 they were strings of the script (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, finding GA2). Its steps:

1. The disk.
2. `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`, and at once the distance stage started in the background.
3. The library order if the build started the caches again, then two copies of the caches for the ladder.
4. `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, never both at once, at four threads, pinned in `build.xml` (P-125, "The suites run Fortress in parallel."). Then `ant testSpecData` once an approved rung brings it into the gate, or the last landed summary has a `specdata/` row; every example must pass (P-124, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.").
5. `summary.txt` from `gate_summary`, one row per suite read from the plain-formatter files under `TEST-RESULTS/`, because the parallel tracks interleave their lines in the ant log. It ends with the `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the machine it ran on (`# machine `, from `rung-flat-tower/machine.sh`), so that timings are read against their machine. The functions are sourced in a call set up whole, its `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` among it: climb batch 26's gate set `FORTRESS_HOME` alone, and its machine lines hold the proxy's 'Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS' line in place of the JDK's and `FORTRESS_THREADS=unset` (`reviews/batch-26-review.md`, process finding 3). `gate_compare` against the newest landed summary: a failure, an empty suite, a count that fell or a suite gone is red. The `system-<i>` shards are compared by their sum, since `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index and a new file moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly that (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`).
6. The four-thread atomic runs: 14 programs, three runs each, 42 lines. A FAIL, NO-PASS or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once.
7. The ladder regression (the skill's `gate.md`): the 85 files of the baseline's pass list compared on phase and output, the `Operation took` line masked, and the eighteen microGPT components compiled only. A DOWN, STDOUT or MISSING line is red unless a rung declared it.
8. The checker count, and 9. the distance, below.

A red gate goes to a judge, then one repair, then one more gate. A gate red after its repair stops the batch, nothing pushed.

### The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage

The gate's step 8 runs the compiler's checker over the interpreter's library (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`, against the stage's 900 s limit; F-240 gives its seconds at the last landed gate) and compares its total with the last landed one. That can run past the Bash tool's 300 s limit, so a rung's worker starts the stage detached with nohup and waits for it with `wait_for`, as the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands", gives them; the distance stage below runs the same way, its seconds in F-240 too. It answers the library route: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37, "The library route."). The total is reported and never red (P-39). A fix can raise it, because the checker stops checking an api at its first errors, and two rungs' changes do not add. `checker_compare` is red only on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow (the instrumented copy no longer matching the tracked checker), or a table with no total. The overloading checker's memo is off in the stage, since it hides 27 to 35 errors depending on build order.

A `testIsStage` rung has that stage as its test: its before is the last landed table, run once after the edit and rebuild. No program can yet be compiled against the interpreter's library, so this is the one place a permanent stage stands in for a test file.

A rung whose every path lies under `explorations/`, `Specification/`, `Documentation/`, a test corpus, the test harness's sources, or walk's evaluator and natives runs neither stage. Both stages run only the compiler's phases (F-111, "The checker-count and distance stages read only the compiler's phases ..."; `STAGE_BLIND`).

### The distance stage

The full measurement of the distance to the switch-over, reported and never red (P-39). `tools/distance/run.sh` runs every stage of the checker over the fourteen components, the twelve prelude components and the two that `List` imports (F-53, F-288), in one JVM, under shadows made from the tracked sources at each run, under the compile command's own setting, read from `Shell.java` at each run, whose implicit bound is `Any` since climb batch 22c (F-289, P-42). An edit that no longer matches stops the run, and `#shadow` says STALE. It starts beside the suites right after `compileAll` and is read last; `compare.sh` prints DISTANCE DOWN, UP or SAME and what moved, and always exits 0. The commit stage lands `distance.txt` and the per-site list, `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which the next batch's rungs read as their before.

- F-229 **`array1` and `array2` give a vector and a matrix only at the eight number types, chosen by a `typecase` over a witness of their result type; at any other element type they give a plain array.** The branches are `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`; each builds the array at that type and returns it through `cast`, in `additiveIdentity`'s shape. `Array1` and `Array2` are invariant, so a branch matches only its own number type exactly. `Number` and `AnyIntegral` get a plain array, since `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not well-formed under the element bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` of `Vector` and `Matrix` (F-151). The specification's "Array Expressions" makes an array of `Number` elements a vector (row 729, contested). Under walk, a type parameter inferred from a `ZZ32` value is `Int`, the one type that `ZZ32` comprises (row 364), and one inferred from a `ZZ64` or `RR64` value is that value's run-time class. Such a type parameter gets a plain array, where the specification gives a vector (row 721). The witness is of the result type because at `T = Int` a witness of the element type, `() -> Int`, would match the `ZZ32` branch, and the `cast` of the `ZZ32` vector to an array of `Int` would throw `CastError`, as `openRange` does (row 722). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayFactoryNumberTypes` and `ArrayFactoryAbstractNumber`. The distance stage measures the compiled checker's acceptance; it reports, and does not turn the gate red. The compiled checker gives a numeral that type; walk still gives it `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-76). Each wider integer type converts from each narrower one, and `RR64` from a `ZZ32` and an `IntLiteral`; a `ZZ64` goes into `RR64` only when written out (P-74). `QQ` converts from the five integer types and `IntLiteral`, and `RR64` converts from `RR32` too (F-139). `NN32` does not yet convert into `RR64`: P-75 decides that it will. `Number`'s `=` compares a float with an exact number after `asFloat`, so it is not transitive (row 434). Under walk, a big operator over a list of numerals, with no static argument on either, such as `SUM <|1, 2, 3|>`, finds no matching overload at run time (row 432), and an empty `SUM` over an additive group that is not a number dies (row 436). ## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. ## 4. What a user gains or loses

1. **With the clause, a user's number type sits beside `Number`, not below it.** It gets the algebra by extending `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing` of itself. The revival's `complex_ring.fss` does so, and writes only `one`, `+`, unary `-`, `TIMES` and `^`. From the traits' defaults it gets binary `-`, `zero` and juxtaposition. It runs today under walk.
2. **What extending `Number` adds beyond that, measured on the complex probe.**
   - Vectors and matrices. `Vector`, `Matrix`, their factories, their products and the norm bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`. Below `Number`, a user's `Cx` gets `vector[\Cx,2\](z)` and `v DOT v`. Under the clause, it cannot be an element type of either.
   - The scalar extension: `v + z`, `z - v`, and `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and one number.
   - Generic code bounded by `Number`: the library's sparse matrices and random generators, the unary `+`, `RR64`'s `^` and `atan2` with a `Number` argument, and `String`'s `||` with a `Number`. The model program's own generics are bounded so too.
   - Exclusion for free. Fifteen of the library's traits exclude `Number` by their own clauses: generators, arrays, ranges, strings, `Maybe`, lists and others. A type below `Number` excludes all of them without writing a clause.
   - `asFloat`. It is abstract on `Number`, so it is an obligation as much as a gain. It is the one explicit conversion into `RR64`.
3. **What extending `Number` brings that is wrong today.** `Number`'s `=` makes any two values of a user's type equal (section 2, point 7). `random(a: Number)` is a native that reads its argument as a float. Both are small repairs, and option (b) lists them.
4. **What the clause gives a user.** It makes `Number` exactly the library's number types. So a user's function on `Number`, defined by cases at the five listed types, is a complete cover for the checker. Without the clause, such a function needs a case for every other number too.
5. **What the exclusion rule and the flat tower need from the clause: nothing, by measurement.** The siblings exclude each other by their own `excludes` clauses: `RR64` excludes `QQ`, `AnyIntegral` and `RR32`; `QQ` excludes `RR64` and `AnyIntegral`; the integer types exclude each other in pairs. They also exclude each other by the exclusion rule, since each is an additive group of itself. `RR32` and `IntLiteral` are objects. The count and the distance stay 0 without the clause.
6. **One part of a record entry no longer holds.** F-151 says that `Number` stays in the array bound because its clause makes the element type exclude `String`. `String` now excludes `Number` and every ring by its own clause, and the checker needs no closure for it. The bound's `Number` still matters for walk's scalar `+` and `-` (section 2, point 7).

The operators \OPR{LSHIFT} and \OPR{RSHIFT} shift the bits of an integer of any of
the five types by a count of any integer type, and return a value of the type of
the integer shifted.
On \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,k)} and
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\VAR{shift}(x,-k)}.
On a fixed-size type of width \VAR{n}, for a nonnegative count \VAR{k},
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k} is \EXP{\lfloor x/2^{k} \rfloor}, and
\EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k} is the value of the type that is congruent to
\EXP{x \cdot 2^{k}} modulo \EXP{2^{n}}: the bits shifted out are lost, and no
\TYP{IntegerOverflow} is thrown.
So a count at or beyond the width gives \EXP{0} for a left shift, and for a right
shift \EXP{0}, or \EXP{-1} if \VAR{x} is negative.
A negative count shifts the other way: \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} (-k)} is
\EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} k}, and \EXP{x \OPR{RSHIFT} (-k)} is \EXP{x \OPR{LSHIFT} k}.
The count is read by its value, whatever its type: an \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} count of
\EXP{2^{63}} or more is beyond the width, not negative.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

content.content:
\subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
\seclabel{revival-comprises}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{natparams}, by the
amendment of 9~October 2026.
\item[Change] The first sentence of a draft note in \secref{trait-decls},
which said that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause are exactly
the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must
explicitly extend it, is replaced by normative text: every listed type
extends the declared trait \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a
value of one of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of
a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain no static variable
other than the static parameters of \VAR{T}; and a trait or object that explicitly extends
\VAR{T} is a subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the same requirement, or
a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends
and every trait or object extending it is a subtype of a listed type.
The note's second sentence, on a clause that includes ``\EXP{\ldots}'', is
kept in its note, and the example of \TYP{Molecule} is unchanged.
The new text answers the third question of Victor Luchangco's draft note
on trait identifiers earlier in the section, whether an instantiation of a
parameterized trait may be listed: it may.
An amendment of 9~October 2026 lets the static arguments of a listed type
contain a \KWD{where}-clause variable of the declaration of \VAR{T} as well,
the listed type then holding at every value of the variable, and adds one
sentence to \secref{natparams}: an argument whose type is a trait whose clause
lists a type at a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} \KWD{where}-clause variable, passed
where that listed type is expected with a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter in
the variable's place, instantiates that parameter, for that call, with the
size of the value itself, a size known to equal only itself.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided it on 28~September 2026.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a \KWD{comprises}
clause as coverage: the clause ``specifies a set of types and generic types
determined by the generic type of the declaration'', and an instantiation of
the declared generic type ``is covered by the union of the types in this set
and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set'', one
generic type $G$ determining another $G'$ ``if every parameter of $G'$ is a
parameter of $G$''
